newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU unveils new Euro coin designs.
newsitem.headline: EU unveils new Euro coin designs.

text.p: The European Union on Monday unveiled the winning designs for the common side of eight new Euro coins, simple arrangements featuring stars and maps of 15-nation bloc which aim to portray European unity.

"I looked at the objectives of the Euro - a united Europe. I tried to symbolise that with maps of Europe," Luc Luycx, the 39-year-old Belgian designer of the coins, told a news conference at the EU's two-day summit in Amsterdam.
"I put the nominal value as big as possible because that's the most important part," he said. Luycx trained as a computer programmer and now designs coins in the Belgian Royal Mint.
His entry was the "clear favourite" chosen from a short list of nine and based on an opinion poll of 2,000 people, a statement released at the news conference said.
The design on the flip side of the coin will be decided by individual countries.
The eight Euro coins will come into circulation by 2002, along with a series of Euro notes whose designs were chosen at the Dublin summit six months ago.

The coins come in denominations of one, two, five cent copper coloured coins, 10, 20 and 50 cent yellow metal coloured coins, and one and two Euro pieces. These last two will have a white coloured metal outer ring and yellow metal inner circle.

The first three show Europe within a globe, the other cent coins have Europe as a collection of nations, and the one and two Euro coins show a borderless bloc. Each features 12 stars and the denomination of the coin in large figures.
The winning design had been favoured by consumer organisations, including the blind and partially sighted, the statement said.

People had liked its clarity and simplicity and 71.2 percent thought it conveyed an idea of Europe as a whole which included each countries heritage, though some had criticised it for being too uniform.
"The winning series of coins aim to be clear, easy-to-use and comprehensible to everyone, portraying the Euro as the currency of Europe, for all Europeans," it said.
It added the new designs were not definitive, but artistic impressions of the coin.

As well as slight adjustments needed to meet recently agreed technical specifications, the map of Europe would be modified "to ensure that all member states are happy with the representation of their country".

French presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said that though European leaders approved the designs at the summit, they had also agreed the Canary Islands should be included in the European maps, after Spain pointed out they were missing.
